questions.q: With inverted dropout (drop probability $p$), a kept unit is multiplied by $\frac{1}{1-p}$. Why?
options: To make the training output larger than the evaluation output
So that the expected activation during training equals the original $h$, and evaluation mode needs no change
To make the variance of the activation equal to zero
Because dropped units must be compensated by negative values
questions.explain: $\mathbb{E}[\tfrac{m}{1-p}h]=\tfrac{(1-p)h}{1-p}=h$. Without the scaling the training activations would on average be only $(1-p)h$, so the test-time network would see a different scale.

questions.q: What does a dropout layer do in evaluation mode (e.g. after `model.eval()` in PyTorch, inverted dropout)?
options: Drops units with probability $p$ as in training
Drops exactly a fraction $p$ of units, chosen deterministically
questions.explain: Inverted dropout already rescaled during training, so at evaluation every unit is kept and passed through unchanged. Classic (non-inverted) dropout instead multiplies by $1-p$ at test time.

questions.q: A layer has $n$ units that can be dropped. How many different sub-networks can dropout sample, and how does evaluation mode relate to them?
options: $2^n$; evaluation mode approximates their average (exactly for a linear model)
$n^2$; evaluation averages them exactly for any network
questions.explain: Each unit is either kept or dropped, giving $2^n$ masks. The page's exact 1,024-mask check shows the ensemble average equals evaluation mode for a linear model but only approximately with a ReLU layer.

questions.q: Why do many large LLM pre-training runs use little or no dropout?
options: Dropout cannot be applied to attention layers
They see huge datasets roughly once, so there is little overfitting to fight and dropout's noise mostly slows learning
questions.explain: Dropout is a regulariser against overfitting. In the single-epoch, trillions-of-tokens regime overfitting is minor, so the extra noise costs more than it helps; dropout is often re-enabled for small fine-tuning datasets.
